title: The white-lipped grove snail
titleCn: 白唇树蜗牛：分布谜题与诺丁汉大学研究

paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
Good afternoon. The topic I've chosen for my presentation is a snail.

Snails belong to a group of animals called mollusks, soft-bodied creatures normally protected by a hard shell. Today, I'm going to talk about a particular example, the white-lipped grove snail, and the research which is being done into it.

I'll start by giving some background information about this variety. The white-lipped snail lives on land and is air-breathing. Its shell is easy to recognize because of its clear stripe, but it varies considerably in color from pale pink to yellow.
The snail gets its rather strange name from the fact that it has a white edge or lip to its shell.
Its principal source of nutrition is plants, which are either already dead or in the process of rotting, a characteristic it shares with a number of other species of snail.
Because of this, its normal habitat is similar to other land snails, and it can be seen in urban settings such as gardens as well as uncultivated areas.
A final point about its ecology is that it also needs calcium and other minerals to keep it healthy. To get these, it frequently consumes soil, which contains these minerals.

So far, nothing I've said would seem to set this variety apart from other land-dwelling, air-breathing snails. However, as long ago as the early nineteenth century, naturalists observed that these white-lipped snails appeared to live in two strikingly separate areas, many hundreds of miles apart, namely Ireland and the Pyrenees, the large mountain range on the border of France and Spain. But what is most surprising is that there was no record of the variety being found anywhere in between these places, so the distribution seemed very strange.

This age-old puzzle has intrigued a group of present-day researchers at the University of Nottingham, and they've decided to undertake a detailed study to investigate the strange distribution pattern.
First of all, they wanted to make sure that the distribution first noticed two hundred years ago is in fact correct.

Via the Internet, they set up what is known as a mega lab, recruiting numerous volunteers across Europe to be responsible for the collection of snail specimens, which were then sent to the university lab.
Like many of these mega lab initiatives, it was generally very successful, with high rates of participation.

The research team then did a genetic analysis of the material they received. They confirmed that there were characteristics shared by the two sets of white-lipped snails from Ireland and from the Pyrenees. Most importantly, this variety does not seem to occur anywhere else.

How could this split have happened, and when? Well, fossils indicate that the white-lipped snail has been living in the Pyrenees for tens of thousands of years, but that in Ireland, its arrival was relatively recent.
This fact was very telling for the researchers. It generated a number of different theories to explain the strange distribution phenomenon.

The first theory the researchers looked at is one called convergent evolution, which basically means that the two sets of snails would have developed entirely separately by complete coincidence. But the underlying similarities between the two sets are too close to be purely a matter of chance, so this seems an unlikely explanation.

The second theory proposed is called natural migration, which would necessitate the snail swimming the sea to Ireland. This was ruled out because they hate salt and simply wouldn't have embarked on the journey across the sea, or had they tried, wouldn't have survived.

The team then started looking at different kinds of evidence, reviewing findings from various locations in the Pyrenees, which showed that mounds of white-lipped snail shells had been thrown away in caves. Clearly, these had been inhabited by Stone Age communities.
This led to the conclusion that the snails must have been used over a long period by these Stone Age humans as food. And interestingly, this was before the advent of agriculture.

The team then looked at other types of archeological evidence from prehistoric times in Ireland and the Pyrenees, and they found evidence that very early on, there had been trade between the people living in these widely separated areas.

For all these reasons, the research team have tentatively concluded that the most likely way in which the snails traveled from east to west was in boats, and that they were transported live to keep them fresh for consumption on the journey.

The research team acknowledged that their study is in the early stages and needs further work. They recognize, for example, that they need to look at a broader sample of the snails. They also feel that other animals and plants might shed light on their research.

They have found that there is probably at least one other type of organism which shows the same distribution pattern, the clear split between the Pyrenees and Ireland. This is a species of tree which they want to look at in more detail. Perhaps its story will corroborate that of the humble migrating white-lipped snail.
